# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Monthly Wholesale Trade

About the Survey

Purpose:

  • To provide month-to-month trends for sales and inventories of U.S. merchant wholesalers, excluding manufacturers' sales branches and offices (MSBOs).
  • Title 13 of the United States Code authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct this survey and provides for voluntary responses.

Content: Companies provide estimates on monthly sales and end-of-month inventories.

Uses:

  • The Bureau of Economic Analysis uses the estimates as an input to estimate sales and inventories for the Gross Domestic Product.
  • The Council of Economic Advisers uses the estimates for assessing near term economic activity.
  • The Department of the Treasury uses the estimates to research economic trends.
  • Business and industry groups use the estimates to forecast future demand.
  • Researchers use the estimates to benchmark the results from their own sampling operations.
  • Manufacturers can use inventory estimates as a proxy for the distributors confidence for future expected sales.

Products:

  • Estimates are released 6 weeks after the close of the data month, containing preliminary current month estimates and final data for the previous month. Statistics include: sales, inventories, and inventories/sales ratios along with standard errors. Estimates are both seasonally adjusted and unadjusted.
  • An annual benchmark report is released each spring. This report presents the results of the benchmarking operation that revises monthly sales and inventories estimates based on the Annual Wholesale Trade Survey. Estimates are both seasonally adjusted and unadjusted.

Frequency: Monthly since 1936. New samples are drawn approximately every 5 years and are updated quarterly. Use of the latest sample began in April 2018.

Coverage: Companies with employment that are primarily engaged in merchant wholesale trade in the U.S, as defined by the 2012 NAICS, excluding MSBOs. Also excluded are non-merchant wholesalers such as agents, brokers, and electronic markets.

Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Monthly Wholesale Trade
Description: The Monthly Wholesale Trade report provides national estimates of monthly sales, inventories, and inventories-to-sales ratios by kind of business for wholesale firms located in the United States (excluding manufacturers' sales branches and offices). Data from this survey provide business leaders and policymakers with an up-to-date picture of the nation's economic condition, and are a key element in estimating the quarterly Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research the Monthly Wholesale Trade dataset comprehensively. Let me start with several searches.I have good foundational information. Let me dig deeper into history, data access, users, and any recent developments.Let me research data access formats, the survey's history, and recent changes.One final search on the survey's status as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator and any recent preservation concerns.# Research Report: Monthly Wholesale Trade (Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey, MWTS)

## Executive Summary

The Monthly Wholesale Trade report is the published output of the **Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey (MWTS)**, conducted by the **U.S. Census Bureau** (an agency of the U.S. Department of Commerce). Your supplied description is **accurate** — it matches, nearly verbatim, the Census Bureau's own official language on the survey's main page (census.gov/wholesale). The survey provides national estimates of monthly sales, end-of-month inventories, and inventories-to-sales ratios for U.S. merchant wholesalers (NAICS sector 42), excluding manufacturers' sales branches and offices (MSBOs). It is one of the Census Bureau's core monthly economic indicators and a principal source of data for the Bureau of Economic Analysis's GDP estimates.

---

## 1. Publisher and Administrative Home

- **Publishing agency:** U.S. Census Bureau, Economic Indicators programs (wholesale trade branch), U.S. Department of Commerce.
- **Main landing page:** https://www.census.gov/wholesale/
- **OMB clearance:** The survey is an approved information collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act, **OMB Control Number 0607-0190**, with respondent forms **SM-4217-A and SM-4217-E**. OMB clearance must be renewed (typically every three years) via Federal Register notice and public comment; recent renewal notices appeared in January 2020 and October 2022.
- **Related surveys in the wholesale program:** the Annual Wholesale Trade Survey (AWTS — now folded into the Annual Integrated Economic Survey, see §6) and the quinquennial Economic Census of Wholesale Trade.

## 2. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Authorizing statute:** **Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182**, which authorize the Census Bureau to conduct current surveys of business between the five-year economic censuses.
- **Response obligation:** **Voluntary.** Unlike the decennial census or the Economic Census (which are mandatory under Title 13 §§ 221–224), response to the MWTS is requested but not legally compelled. This is a notable point for policy advocates: the survey's continuity depends heavily on respondent cooperation and on maintaining respondent trust and low burden.
- **Confidentiality protections:** Respondent data are protected under **Title 13 § 9** — usable only for statistical purposes, never publishable in a form that identifies an individual business, and immune from legal process. All persons with access are sworn under Title 13 and subject to criminal penalties for disclosure. Data transmission systems are additionally screened under the **Federal Cybersecurity Enhancement Act of 2015**.
- **Burden disclosure:** Per the 2022 Federal Register notice, the survey covers ~4,200 respondents, estimated at **7 minutes per monthly response**, totaling roughly **5,880 annual burden hours**, with $0 estimated direct cost to the public.

## 3. History

- **Origins:** The survey has been conducted **monthly since 1936** according to the Census Bureau's current overview page (a legacy Census page states "monthly since 1939" — a minor discrepancy in the Bureau's own documentation, likely reflecting a pre-war start date versus resumption/regularization; the 1936 figure is the officially published one).
- **Sample redesigns:** New probability samples are drawn approximately **every five years**, updated quarterly for business births, deaths, and other universe changes. The current sample was introduced with **April 2018** data and restated the full series on **2012 NAICS** definitions (prior-sample estimates on 2007 NAICS were backcast for continuity).
- **NAICS era:** The published time series begins in **January 1992** on a NAICS basis (one detailed series, Computer and Computer Peripheral Equipment wholesalers, begins January 1997). Pre-1992 data exist on the older SIC basis in archived reports.
- **Benchmark lineage:** Monthly estimates are benchmarked to annual totals (formerly AWTS, benchmarked in turn to the Economic Census of Wholesale Trade in years ending in 2 and 7). The most recent major revision (released 2024) benchmarked MWTS estimates to the **2022 AWTS**, itself benchmarked to the **2017 Economic Census**, revising not-adjusted sales estimates from January 2013 forward and seasonally adjusted estimates from January 2010 forward.
- **Product innovations:**
  - **July 28, 2016:** Introduction of the **Advance Economic Indicators Report**, releasing advance wholesale (and retail) inventory aggregates ~27 days after the reference month, developed in collaboration with BEA to reduce revisions to the advance GDP estimate.
  - **September 19, 2022:** Launch of the experimental **Monthly Real Dollar Estimates of Wholesale Sales**, deflating nominal MWTS sales using BLS price indexes and Census product weights (available from January 2012).

## 4. Methodology (for Data Scientists)

- **Universe/sampling frame:** Employer businesses (identified by IRS Employer Identification Numbers, EINs) on the Census Bureau's **Business Register** that are classified as merchant wholesalers — firms that take title to the goods they sell (jobbers, industrial distributors, exporters, importers, drop shippers). **Excluded:** manufacturers' sales branches and offices (MSBOs, covered instead by the M3 manufacturers' survey) and NAICS 4251 (agents, brokers, wholesale electronic markets).
- **Sample design:** Stratified one-stage design; **42 primary strata** by kind of business, substratified into 4–13 annual-sales-size strata per industry. The largest-size stratum in each industry is sampled with certainty. Sample ≈ **4,200–4,400 businesses** (~1,700 certainty companies and ~2,500–2,700 noncertainty EINs); sampling weights range from 1 to 500, set to meet coefficient-of-variation targets on annual sales and year-end inventory totals.
- **Data items:** Monthly sales, end-of-month inventories, number of establishments covered, and the reporting period end date (if not a calendar month). Collection by mail, fax, internet, and telephone.
- **Estimation:** Horvitz–Thompson (weighted) totals; imputation for unit/item nonresponse using similar-sized firms in the same industry; variances by the **random groups method**; published standard errors and coefficients of variation.
- **Revision cycle:** Preliminary estimates ~40 days after the data month, finalized ~30 days later; annual benchmarking each spring constrains monthly sums to annual survey totals and applies a "carry-forward factor" to post-benchmark months; sample-to-sample linkage uses geometric-mean ratio methods.
- **Seasonal adjustment:** Census Bureau's **X-13ARIMA-SEATS** program (X-11 filter-based procedure), with trading-day adjustment. Both seasonally adjusted and not-seasonally-adjusted series are published.
- **Geography:** **National estimates only** — there is no state or subnational detail, a common point of confusion for new users.

## 5. Data Products and Access (for Data Librarians and Preservationists)

**Release schedule (three monthly touchpoints):**
1. **Advance Economic Indicators Report** — ~27 days after month-end; aggregate wholesale inventories only.
2. **Monthly Wholesale Trade report (full)** — ~39–42 days after month-end; sales, inventories, and inventories/sales ratios with standard errors.
3. **Manufacturing and Trade Inventories and Sales (MTIS)** — ~45 days after month-end; combined manufacturing, wholesale, and retail.
4. **Annual revision/benchmark report** — each spring.

**Access channels:**
- **Census Data API:** `https://api.census.gov/data/timeseries/eits/mwts` — part of the Economic Indicator Time Series API family; free, key required.
- **Time Series/Trend Charts tool:** census.gov/econ/currentdata/?programCode=MWTS — interactive extraction with bulk download.
- **Static files:** Current and historic reports in PDF and Excel at census.gov/wholesale and www2.census.gov (e.g., the current report at /wholesale/pdf/mwts/currentwhl.pdf).
- **Third-party mirror:** **FRED** (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), release ID 290, "Monthly Wholesale Trade: Sales and Inventories" — 220+ series (88 sales, 88 inventories, 44 ratios), each in adjusted and unadjusted form, from January 1992 forward. FRED provides an independent replication and API path, useful both for convenience and redundancy.

**⚠ Critical preservation note — two distinct historical file series:** The Census Bureau explicitly distinguishes:
- **Historic release files:** the reports *as originally released* — never updated. These preserve the real-time data vintages.
- **Historic time series files:** updated every month (current preliminary estimates added; prior month finalized).

For preservation and for "real-time data" research (e.g., replicating what policymakers actually saw at the time), the **historic release files are the essential artifact**, because benchmarking and seasonal-adjustment revisions continuously rewrite the time series. Any archiving effort should capture both, plus the annual benchmark revision reports that document the revision methodology (e.g., the 2024 revisions notice PDF).

**Format risks:** Data are distributed primarily as PDF, XLS/XLSX, and through web tools and APIs — all service-dependent. There is no bulk open-data dump of full vintages outside the website; the API serves current (revised) values, not historical vintages. The FRED/ALFRED ecosystem (ALFRED stores vintages) is the de facto archival backstop.

## 6. Ecosystem and Recent Structural Changes

- **AWTS sunset / AIES transition:** The Annual Wholesale Trade Survey — the MWTS's benchmarking source — was **sunset after survey year 2022** and absorbed into the new **Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES)**, which consolidated seven annual business surveys (ARTS, AWTS, SAS, ASM, ACES, M3UFO, Report of Organization) to reduce respondent burden. AIES began data collection in **March 2024** (survey year 2023). The MWTS continues as a standalone monthly indicator but will now be benchmarked to AIES results; the next benchmark revision (to 2023/2024 AIES estimates) was tentatively scheduled for **October 26, 2026**. This transition is the single most important near-term continuity issue for the series.
- **Industry classification risk:** The current series rests on 2012 NAICS; a future migration to a newer NAICS vintage would trigger another restatement, as happened in 2018.
- **Budget/statistical-system context:** As a voluntary survey with ~5,880 burden hours, the MWTS is relatively inexpensive, but like all federal statistical products it depends on Census Bureau appropriations, OMB clearance cycles, and the integrity of the Business Register (which relies on IRS administrative data).

## 7. Typical Users and Public Benefits

**Government users:**
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** The flagship use. MWTS data are the primary input for estimating **change in private inventories** and **nonfarm proprietors' income** in GDP. The full MWTS report feeds BEA's **second and third GDP estimates**; the Advance Economic Indicators Report was created specifically so BEA could use real inventory data (rather than an assumption) for the third month of the quarter in its **advance GDP estimate**, measurably reducing revisions.
- **Council of Economic Advisers:** near-term economic assessment.
- **Department of the Treasury:** economic trend research.
- **Federal Reserve Board:** timely reading on current economic performance (inventories are a key cyclical indicator).
- **Bureau of Labor Statistics:** input to **Producer Price Indexes** and productivity measures.

**Private-sector and research users:**
- Businesses and trade/industry associations forecasting demand and benchmarking their own surveys.
- Manufacturers using wholesale inventory levels as a proxy for distributor confidence in future sales.
- Financial analysts and economists tracking the business cycle — the inventories/sales ratio is a widely watched indicator of supply-chain tightness and turning points (it spiked notably in the 2008–09 recession and again during the 2020–22 pandemic disruptions).
- Academic researchers, including real-time data and GDP-nowcasting studies (the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow and similar models consume wholesale inventory data).

**Public benefit case (for policy activists):**
- MWTS is the **only continuous measure** of monthly wholesale sales and inventories in the U.S. economy (per the Census Bureau's own OMB justification). Wholesale trade is the connective tissue between manufacturers and retailers; without it, GDP inventory estimates — one of the most volatile and consequential GDP components — would rest on assumptions.
- It underpins monetary and fiscal decisions that affect employment, interest rates, and program funding; disruptions or degradations propagate directly into GDP quality, as BEA's documentation of the 2016 advance-report improvement illustrates.
- Respondent burden is minimal (7 minutes/month, voluntary), making it a high-value, low-burden statistical product — a strong talking point for defending funding.

## 8. Quick Reference

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| Official name | Monthly Wholesale Trade Survey (MWTS) |
| Publisher | U.S. Census Bureau, Dept. of Commerce |
| Authority | Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 131, 182 (voluntary response); confidentiality under § 9 |
| OMB control no. | 0607-0190 (forms SM-4217-A / SM-4217-E) |
| Frequency | Monthly since 1936; published series from Jan 1992 (NAICS basis) |
| Coverage | U.S. merchant wholesalers (NAICS 42), excl. MSBOs and NAICS 4251; national only |
| Sample | ~4,200–4,400 firms; stratified probability sample; redesigned ~every 5 years (latest: April 2018) |
| Key outputs | Sales, end-of-month inventories, inventories/sales ratios; SA and NSA; standard errors |
| Release timing | Advance inventories ~day 27; full report ~day 39–42; MTIS ~day 45; annual benchmark each spring |
| Access | Census API (timeseries/eits/mwts), time-series tool, PDF/XLS, FRED release 290 |
| Related datasets | AIES (formerly AWTS) benchmark source; Economic Census of Wholesale Trade; MTIS; Advance Economic Indicators |
| Watch items | 2026 AIES-based benchmark revision; vintage preservation (historic release files vs. time series files); voluntary-response dependence |

**Sources consulted:** Census Bureau MWTS overview, methodology, respondent, FAQ, and revisions pages (census.gov/wholesale); Federal Register OMB clearance notices (2020, 2022, 2023, 2024); BEA NIPA Handbook Chapter 3 and BEA FAQ on advance inventories; Census Bureau AIES/AWTS transition pages; FRED release documentation; Title 13 U.S.C.

Now let me check Census Bureau leadership changes, budget trajectory, and the staffing tracker.# Risk Assessment: Monthly Wholesale Trade (MWTS), U.S. Census Bureau

**Assessment date context:** Research conducted using sources through October 2026. The most recent release found is the August 2026 report (released October 8, 2026), and the survey's OMB clearance was renewed April 3, 2026 through April 30, 2029.

---

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **Gone / High Risk:** No evidence. Historic release files (as-originally-published vintages, e.g., `mwts_202508.pdf`) and historic time series files remain posted at www2.census.gov; the API (`timeseries/eits/mwts`) and the Time Series/Trend Charts tool remain live; FRED (release ID 290) continues to mirror 220+ series back to January 1992.
- **Moderate Risk:** No evidence of any data elements being removed from the MWTS series. The only removals at Census in 2025 involved unrelated demographic/DEI-adjacent content, not economic indicator programs.
- **No Known Issue:** All vintages from January 1992 forward (plus pre-NAICS archived reports) remain accessible with no known alterations; redundant third-party archiving exists via FRED/ALFRED.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** I found no removal or alteration of historical MWTS data, files, or elements. The 2025 shutdown delayed but did not delete anything. Minor caveat: the Senate Appropriations Committee's FY2026 report language directing Census to report on "the removal of Census and BEA data sets" confirms removals have occurred *somewhere* in the Bureau, so continued monitoring is warranted — but nothing has touched this dataset.

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **Gone / High Risk:** Collection and publication have not been terminated. The ICR (OMB 0607-0190) was renewed as a routine "Extension without change," concluded by OIRA **April 3, 2026**, expiring **April 30, 2029** — renewed *before* the prior April 30, 2026 expiration (Federal Register 90 FR 39180, Aug. 14, 2025; 90 FR 56716, Dec. 8, 2025; reginfo.gov ICR ref. 202511-0607-001). The October 2025 shutdown did not cause permanent gaps: Census's published *Recovery Plan for Census' Principal Federal Economic Indicators* committed to processing all missed/delayed reference periods chronologically to deliver "complete and continuous time series."
- **Moderate Risk:** **Criterion met.** The October 1–November 12, 2025 lapse in appropriations forced missed publication dates: the August 2025 MWTS report (normally ~October 9) was delayed to November 21, 2025, with the release itself noting "Next release: To be determined. Report delayed due to recent lapse in federal funding." No collection or processing occurred for the October reference period during the lapse, and the schedule took months to recover (catch-up completed in 2026; the August 2026 report was back on normal cadence, released October 8, 2026). There is no statutory publication deadline protecting the schedule, and further funding lapses remain a live possibility.
- **No Known Issue:** Supported by the active ICR, restored release cadence, scheduled AIES benchmark revision (tentatively October 26, 2026), and continued three-product release family (Advance Indicators, full MWTS, MTIS).

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** The rubric's plain language is decisive: the "typical or intended publication date" was missed and "collection or publication [was] delayed" within the past year. The cause was a government-wide funding lapse rather than agency action, and recovery is complete — but the dataset demonstrated vulnerability to exactly the kind of disruption this category measures, and there is no statutory backstop for the release schedule. The ICR itself is in excellent shape.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **Gone / High Risk:** Not met. No documented reduction in MWTS granularity (full kind-of-business detail), frequency (monthly), or products; seasonally adjusted and unadjusted series, standard errors, and the experimental real-dollar estimates all continue.
- **Moderate Risk:** **Criterion met.** (a) The sister M3 survey in the same economic indicators program area announced in 2026 that "due to schedule and resource constraints," revised historical data and seasonal adjustment models "will remain unchanged for the remainder of [2026]" — direct evidence that resource constraints are now forcing quality compromises in this program family. (b) The PFEI recovery plan explicitly shortened collection windows (10→7 business days) and compressed review/analysis time, flagging nonresponse risks — a temporary but real quality pressure. (c) MWTS is a **voluntary** survey dependent on ~4,200 respondents; politicization of statistics and respondent-trust erosion is a recognized emerging risk to response rates.
- **No Known Issue:** Supported by unchanged published methodology, continued X-13ARIMA-SEATS adjustment, and the planned 2026 benchmark to AIES.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** No actual degradation of MWTS outputs has been documented, but the rubric's "potential or emerging risk" language squarely covers the observed resource-constraint notices in the same directorate, compressed processing protocols, and staffing losses that thin the margins of error management.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **High Risk:** Not met. Authorization is explicit, not vague: Title 13 U.S.C. §§ 131 and 182 are named on every form and Federal Register notice. There is **no substitute collection** — Census's own OMB justification calls MWTS "the only continuous measure of monthly wholesale sales, end-of-month inventories, and inventories-to-sales ratios." Programmatic use is intense and institutionalized: BEA requires the data for GDP change-in-private-inventories and nonfarm proprietors' income (NIPA Handbook Ch. 3); the Advance Economic Indicators Report exists specifically to serve BEA's advance GDP estimate.
- **Moderate Risk:** Arguably applicable on a technicality: the survey is *authorized* rather than *explicitly required* by statute (response is voluntary; no statutory publication deadline exists, as the 2025 shutdown demonstrated). But it is required for implementation of a federal program (GDP estimation) with no substitutes.
- **No Known Issue:** **Best fit.** Statutory authorization is explicitly named (13 U.S.C. §§ 131, 182); the collection scope is well-specified; no alternative collection could substitute; and it is load-bearing for GDP, a federal program. Congress reinforced this in the enacted FY2026 CJS bill (P.L. 119-74), which funded Current Economic Statistics above the Administration's request.

**Selected level: No Known Issue.** The statutory footing is about as strong as a current (intercensal) business survey can have. Flag for preservationists: because publication timing is discretionary and response is voluntary, legal protection covers the *authority to collect*, not a guaranteed release schedule.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **Gone:** Not remotely met; the Bureau is funded (FY2026 enacted: $1.490 billion, +$108M over FY2025) and operating.
- **High Risk:** **Criteria met on staffing.** The Census Bureau has lost an estimated **~1,500 staff since January 2025** via deferred resignations (AFGE Council 241, via Bloomberg Law) — crossing the rubric's **1,000+ staff** threshold — and an estimated **15% of total staffing since FY2024** (American Statistical Association, *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*). Additional ~100 RIF notices went to a Tucson call center during the shutdown. The FY2026 President's Budget Request envisioned a 9% further staffing decline (7,657 FTE) and a 27% cut to periodic-census staffing. Leadership has turned over twice since January 2025 (Director Robert Santos resigned February 14, 2025; career acting director Ron Jarmin was replaced in September 2025 by political appointee George Cook as acting director).
- **Moderate Risk:** Also defensible if weighted on percentages: 15% staffing loss falls in the 10–39% band; the enacted FY2026 budget was *not* cut (Current Surveys and Programs account: $319M, only ~$10M/3% below FY2025, and $30M above the request); leadership was changed rather than "threatened."
- **No Known Issue:** Not supportable given the above.

**Selected level: High Risk.** The rubric's disjunctive criteria are explicit: "1,000 or more staff lost" is sufficient, and ~1,500 documented losses exceed it. I also weigh the operational amplifiers: a government-wide hiring freeze (only partially waived for Census), a Commerce policy requiring Secretary-level approval of contracts over $100,000 that created a backlog of 3,000+ requests, and hiring now restricted to one-for-four attrition. Mitigant: Congress *rejected* the proposed 12.3% cut to Current Surveys and Programs, so the funding pillar of this category is currently stable — the rating rests on staffing losses and leadership instability, not budget.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence by risk level:**

- **Gone / High Risk:** Not met for this dataset. The December 2025 ICR was an ordinary extension **without change**, not a Presidential Action-driven ICR. There is no negative policy note on census.gov/wholesale. No changes to MWTS content, methodology, or release practice have been made pursuant to Administration priorities. Unlike BLS (commissioner fired after a jobs report) or ERS (report delayed/redacted for its trade-deficit findings), there is **no evidence of political interference with MWTS releases**.
- **Moderate Risk:** **Criterion met.** Proposed/pending structural changes: the FY2026 budget "supports the President's Budget proposal to reorganize the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Bureau of Economic Analysis, and the Census Bureau at the Department of Commerce" — a major, unresolved reorganization affecting the producing agency. The Commerce Department terminated Census's federal advisory committees (including the Census Scientific Advisory Committee) by Federal Register notice June 10, 2025. Administration statements on excluding undocumented people from the census and the August 2025 directive show willingness to direct statistical operations by presidential action.
- **No Known Issue:** Not supportable — notable administration-driven changes since January 2025 (advisory committee terminations, reorganization proposal, SIPP restructuring) affect the Bureau that produces this dataset, even though MWTS itself is untouched.

**Selected level: Moderate Risk.** MWTS has been conspicuously *unaffected* — likely because it is a low-salience, business-friendly indicator whose renewal the Administration processed routinely. But the rubric asks about proposed or pending changes and official statements suggesting change; the BLS/BEA/Census reorganization proposal and the demonstrated pattern of intervention elsewhere in the statistical system keep this at Moderate. Wholesale inventory data is also more politically salient than usual given tariff policy, which slightly elevates the tail risk of future attention.

---

## Overall Notes for Preservationists

- **Biggest near-term watch items:** (1) recurrence of funding lapses; (2) the October 2026 AIES-based benchmark revision — a large, legitimate revision event that will rewrite history; preservationists should snapshot pre-revision files *now*; (3) the M3 "resource constraints" precedent spreading to other indicators.
- **Redundancy is good but not complete:** FRED/ALFRED mirrors the series (and ALFRED retains vintages), but the unique artifacts at risk are the Census **historic release files** (as-originally-released PDFs/XLS) and methodology/benchmark documentation — these have no complete third-party mirror.
- **Systemic context:** The dataset's risks are almost entirely *institutional* (staffing, leadership, funding continuity) rather than *political targeting* — MWTS has no culture-war exposure, which materially lowers its profile compared to demographic datasets.

## Summary of Risk Levels

- **Historical Data Availability: No Known Issue**
- **Future Data Availability: Moderate Risk** (2025 shutdown caused missed publication dates and delayed collection; recovered; ICR active through 4/30/2029)
- **Data Quality: Moderate Risk** (no MWTS degradation yet; resource-constraint notices and compressed processing in the program area signal emerging risk)
- **Statutory Context: No Known Issue** (explicit Title 13 §§ 131/182 authorization; sole source; required for GDP)
- **Staffing and Funding: High Risk** (~1,500 staff lost since Jan 2025, ~15% of workforce; hiring freeze; leadership turnover — though enacted FY2026 funding is stable)
- **Policy: Moderate Risk** (MWTS itself untouched; pending Census/BLS/BEA reorganization proposal and terminated advisory committees; no interference with this series to date)
